The primary stand of the insurance company is that the person driving the vehicle did not have a
valid driving license. In Swaran Singh's case (supra) the following situations were noted:
(i) the driver had a license but it was fake;

(ii) the driver had no license at all;
(iii) the driver originally had a valid license but it had expired as on the date of the
accident and had not been renewed;
(iv) the license was for a class of vehicles other than that which was the insured
vehicle;
(v) the license was a learner's license.
Category (i) may cover two types of situations. First, the license itself was fake and the second is
where originally that license is fake but there has been a renewal subsequently in accordance with
law.
Chapter II contains Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act relating to licensing of drivers driving the motor
vehicles.
Where the claim relates to own damage claims, it cannot be adjudicated by the insurance company.
But it has to be decided by an other forum i.e. forum created under the Consumer Protection Act,
1985 (in short the 'CP Act'). Before the Tribunal, there were essentially three parties i.e. the insurer,
insured and the claimants. On the contrary, before the consumer forums there were two parties i.e.
owner of the vehicle and the insurer. The claimant does not come in to the picture. Therefore, these
are cases where there is no third party involved.
According to learned counsel for the appellants, in such cases the logic i.e. let the insurer pay and
recover from the insured company does not apply.
As noted above, there is no contractual relation between the third party and the insurer. Because of
the statutory intervention in terms of Section 149, the same becomes operative in essence and
Section 149 provides complete insulation.
In the background of the statutory provisions, one thing is crystal clear i.e. the statute is beneficial
one qua the third party.

egislative purpose."
More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

The inevitable conclusion therefore is that the decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no
application to own damage cases. The effect of fake license has to be considered in the light of what
has been stated by this Court in New India Assurance Co., Shimla v. Kamla and Ors. (2001 (4) SCC
342). Once the license is a fake one the renewal cannot take away the effect of fake license. It was
observed in Kamla's case (supra) as follows:
"12. As a point of law we have no manner of doubt that a fake licence cannot get its
forgery outfit stripped off merely on account of some officer renewing the same with
or without knowing it to be forged. Section 15 of the Act only empowers any Licensing
Authority to "renew a driving licence issued under the provisions of this Act with
effect from the date of its expiry". No Licensing Authority has the power to renew a
fake licence and, therefore, a renewal if at all made cannot transform a fake licence as
genuine. Any counterfeit document showing that it contains a purported order of a
statutory authority would ever remain counterfeit albeit the fact that other persons
including some statutory authorities would have acted on the document unwittingly
on the assumption that it is genuine".
As noted above, the conceptual difference between third party right and own damage cases has to be
kept in view. Initially, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the license was a fake one.

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the licence appears genuine and the driver is competent, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner hired a driver who produced a licence with an LMV + transport vehicle endorsement. The court held the owner had done enough — he was not required to verify whether the endorsement covered the specific sub-class of heavy goods vehicle.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most directly applicable authority on the scope of the owner's verification duty. It quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 verbatim and applies it to hold that the owner's obligation is satisfied by a prima facie check of the licence document.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. ... Thus where the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently there would be no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory under Section 149. Even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), the insurer must pay the third party and can recover from the insured. The breach must be on the part of the insured — the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a valid licence to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The court still held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights, reaffirming that the breach must be 'willful' on the owner's part.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where there IS a licence defect, the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim — it only entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The owner's failure to check does not let the insurer off the hook to third parties.
supporting.quote: As held in Skandia and Sohan Lal Passi cases the breach must be on the part of the insured. ... If it ultimately turns out that the licence was fake, the insurance company would continue to remain liable unless they prove that the owner/insured was aware or had noticed that the licence was fake and still permitted that person to drive.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds a valid LMV licence but lacks a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle, the insurer cannot avoid third-party liability. The owner is not expected to know the fine distinctions between licence classes.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had an LMV licence but no badge/endorsement for a tourist maxi cab (commercial vehicle). The Supreme Court held the insurer liable, rejecting the argument that the owner should have checked for the endorsement.
supporting.why_it_matters: Limits the owner's verification duty: the owner need not check for specific endorsements or badges that are matters of regulatory detail. A licence that on its face authorises the relevant class of vehicle is sufficient.
supporting.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: An expired licence that is subsequently renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer remains liable and must pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed later. The court held the insurer liable to third parties, finding no fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even where the licence had lapsed (a clear defect an owner could have spotted by checking the expiry date), the insurer's defence does not succeed against third parties. The owner's failure to notice an expired licence does not defeat the claim.
supporting.quote: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no badge for tourist maxi cab. The court applied pay-and-recover, holding the insurer liable to the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the owner failed to ensure the driver had the correct endorsement/badge, the insurer's defence does not defeat the third-party claim — it only shifts the ultimate burden to the owner via recovery.
supporting.quote: The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any licence at all is a fundamental and statutory breach. However, even in such cases, the insurer must pay the third party first and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal found a fundamental breach but still applied pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — does not allow the insurer to escape liability to the third party. The insurer must pay and then recover. This confirms that failing to check (even where the driver has no licence) does not defeat the insurer's defence in the sense of avoiding payment to the claimant.
supporting.quote: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a special endorsement is required (e.g., for carrying hazardous goods), the owner has a duty under Rule 132(5) of the CMVR to ensure the driver holds the requisite endorsement. Absence of such endorsement is a breach entitling the insurer to pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The vehicle was a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The driver had a valid HGV/HTV licence but no special endorsement under Rule 9 CMVR. The court held the owner failed in his duty and granted pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the one case where the court specifically identified a positive duty on the owner (under Rule 132(5) CMVR) to verify a special endorsement. It shows that where the law specifically casts a duty on the owner to verify a particular licence condition, failure to do so is a breach — but still results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: Swaran Singh's pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks under Section 149. It does NOT apply to own-damage claims or disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side (claimant) will not cite this — it helps the insurer. But the insurer's own counsel must be aware: if the claim is an own-damage claim (not a third-party claim), the pay-and-recover safety net disappears. The insurer can fully defend on licence grounds.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about own-damage claims and consumer forum disputes between insurer and insured. In third-party claims (which are the vast majority of motor accident cases), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover principle fully apply. The claimant will not be affected by this limitation.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
adverse.principle: Where a licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date. The insurer must pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even a lapsed licence does not defeat the claim — the insurer must still pay. The risk is that the court may treat this as a breach that shifts ultimate liability to the owner via recovery, but the insurer still pays first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position that there IS a breach (licence not valid on accident date). The pay-and-recover order protects the third party but gives the insurer full recovery rights against the owner. The insurer's defence succeeds in the sense that the owner bears the ultimate burden.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any licence is a fundamental breach. The insurer is not directly liable but must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must still pay. This is the strongest case for the claimant on the 'pay first' point.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case confirms the insurer's ultimate right to recover from the owner. The insurer's defence is not 'defeated' — it succeeds in shifting the burden to the owner. The insurer pays only as a statutory conduit to protect the third party.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will rely heavily on this for the proposition that licence defects do not let the insurer off the hook to third parties. The insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case explicitly reaffirms that the breach must be 'on the part of the insured' — i.e., the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver. If the owner checked and the licence appeared genuine, there is no 'breach' at all, and the insurer cannot even recover. This cuts both ways.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid third-party liability merely because the driver of an LMV did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the owner's duty to verify does not extend to checking for specific endorsements or badges. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This actually helps the insurer's position on the scope of the owner's duty — it confirms the owner need not check for regulatory endorsements. The insurer's defence (that the owner should have checked for a badge) is weakened, but the insurer still gets pay-and-recover.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: An expired licence that is renewed later does not constitute a fundamental breach. The insurer is liable to third parties.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even an expired licence (which the owner could have spotted) does not defeat the claim. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case is distinguishable on timing — the licence was renewed shortly after the accident, and the court emphasised that the licensing authority cannot refuse renewal within 5 years. The insurer still gets recovery rights against the owner.

priority_arguments: Lead with the Lehru principle (as quoted in Chennamma/doc_027): the owner's duty is limited to checking whether the licence 'on the face of it looks genuine'. The owner is NOT expected to verify with the RTO or investigate whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority.

Argue that if the owner checked the licence and it appeared genuine, and the driver demonstrated competence, there is NO breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii) at all — the insurer cannot even recover from the owner, let alone avoid liability.

In the alternative, argue that even if there IS a breach (e.g., no licence, fake licence, expired licence), the insurer's remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. This is settled law from Swaran Singh through to the present corpus.

Distinguish between third-party claims (where pay-and-recover applies) and own-damage claims (where Laxmi Narain Dhut/doc_031 limits Swaran Singh). In third-party claims, the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim.

Where the licence defect is a missing endorsement or badge (not absence of a licence altogether), rely on S.Iyyapan/doc_032 to argue that the owner cannot be expected to verify regulatory endorsements — the licence on its face was sufficient.

Where the licence had expired but was later renewed, rely on Srinivasamurthy/doc_034 and Parvathi Hebbar/doc_003 to argue that while there is a breach (licence not valid on accident date), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: The claimant will argue that the owner failed in his duty to verify the licence, and this constitutes a 'breach' that at least entitles the insurer to recover from the owner. If the owner is impecunious or untraceable, the insurer may be left bearing the loss despite having a recovery order.

In own-damage claims (not third-party), Laxmi Narain Dhut/doc_031 holds that Swaran Singh does not apply — the insurer can fully defend on licence grounds. Ensure the claim is properly characterised as a third-party claim.

If the owner did not check the licence AT ALL (e.g., hired a driver without asking for a licence), the court may find this is a 'willful' breach, strengthening the insurer's recovery rights but also potentially exposing the insurer to arguments that the owner was negligent.

The Sunil Shreesail Killiket/doc_024 case shows that even a 'fundamental breach' (no licence at all) results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer should not overstate the strength of its defence — it will have to pay first in third-party claims.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party motor accident claims before the MACT, the insurer should: (1) plead the licence defect specifically; (2) lead evidence to prove the defect (RTO verification report, MV Inspector testimony); (3) seek a pay-and-recover order against the owner/driver; (4) NOT argue for complete exoneration from third-party liability, as the corpus uniformly rejects this. In own-damage claims (consumer forum or civil suit), the insurer can take the full defence under Laxmi Narain Dhut.

caveats: This analysis is limited to the 56-judgment corpus provided. Key Supreme Court precedents like Swaran Singh, Lehru, Skandia, and Sohan Lal Passi are cited within the corpus judgments but are not themselves part of the corpus. Their principles are applied through the corpus judgments.

The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely exonerated from third-party liability on licence grounds. Every licence-defect case in the corpus results in pay-and-recover. This may reflect a selection bias in the corpus rather than the full range of possible outcomes.
doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is an insurer-favouring judgment but is limited to own-damage claims. It does not help the insurer in third-party claims.

doc_002 (Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi) and doc_007 (National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Harpreet Singh) are insurer-favouring outcomes but appear to involve different issues (gratuitous passengers, etc.) and were not read in detail as they are not directly on the licence-verification point.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Punjab & Haryana At Chandigarh
payload.holding: The criminal revision petition is partly allowed by upholding the conviction of the petitioner under Sections 279, 337, 304-A, and 427 of the IPC, but modifying the substantive sentence for the offence under Section 304-A IPC from two years of rigorous imprisonment to 18 months, while maintaining the other sentences and fine.
payload.ratio: In-court identification by eyewitnesses is valid and admissible in law even without a prior Test Identification Parade, provided the witnesses had sufficient opportunity to observe the accused. 15. Now we shall examine the second aspect of the case. In order to establish criminal
liability the "rash or negligent" act by the accused is to be established the prosecution.
The prosecution has to prove that that the negligence or rashness of the accused went

(O&M) Mohammed Aynuddin @ Miyam vs State of Andhra 2000(3) RCR (Crl.) 619,
the Apex Court has held that:

presumed. To constitute either of the offence under section 279 IPC or section 304-A
IPC, the proof of criminal rashness or criminal negligence is essential. Even in
ordinary parlance 'negligence' connotes want of proper care and 'rashness' conveys
the idea of recklessness or doing of an act without due consideration. The rashness or
negligence must be described as criminal rashness or criminal negligence. "
16. The learned counsel for the appellant/accused has contended that the mere deposition of the
eye-witnesses is insufficient to conclusively establish that the accused was driving the vehicle in a
rash and negligent manner. However, I find no merit in this contention. In the present case, the
prosecution's consistent case is that the deceased Balbir was proceeding from his pushcart (rehri)

PW-6 was the son of the deceased, assisting his father in his daily vocation, while PW-7 was a

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the licence appears genuine and the driver is competent, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner hired a driver who produced a licence with an LMV + transport vehicle endorsement. The court held the owner had done enough — he was not required to verify whether the endorsement covered the specific sub-class of heavy goods vehicle.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most directly applicable authority on the scope of the owner's verification duty. It quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 verbatim and applies it to hold that the owner's obligation is satisfied by a prima facie check of the licence document.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. ... Thus where the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently there would be no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory under Section 149. Even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), the insurer must pay the third party and can recover from the insured. The breach must be on the part of the insured — the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a valid licence to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The court still held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights, reaffirming that the breach must be 'willful' on the owner's part.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where there IS a licence defect, the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim — it only entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The owner's failure to check does not let the insurer off the hook to third parties.
supporting.quote: As held in Skandia and Sohan Lal Passi cases the breach must be on the part of the insured. ... If it ultimately turns out that the licence was fake, the insurance company would continue to remain liable unless they prove that the owner/insured was aware or had noticed that the licence was fake and still permitted that person to drive.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds a valid LMV licence but lacks a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle, the insurer cannot avoid third-party liability. The owner is not expected to know the fine distinctions between licence classes.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had an LMV licence but no badge/endorsement for a tourist maxi cab (commercial vehicle). The Supreme Court held the insurer liable, rejecting the argument that the owner should have checked for the endorsement.
supporting.why_it_matters: Limits the owner's verification duty: the owner need not check for specific endorsements or badges that are matters of regulatory detail. A licence that on its face authorises the relevant class of vehicle is sufficient.
supporting.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: An expired licence that is subsequently renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer remains liable and must pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed later. The court held the insurer liable to third parties, finding no fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even where the licence had lapsed (a clear defect an owner could have spotted by checking the expiry date), the insurer's defence does not succeed against third parties. The owner's failure to notice an expired licence does not defeat the claim.
supporting.quote: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no badge for tourist maxi cab. The court applied pay-and-recover, holding the insurer liable to the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the owner failed to ensure the driver had the correct endorsement/badge, the insurer's defence does not defeat the third-party claim — it only shifts the ultimate burden to the owner via recovery.
supporting.quote: The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any licence at all is a fundamental and statutory breach. However, even in such cases, the insurer must pay the third party first and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal found a fundamental breach but still applied pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — does not allow the insurer to escape liability to the third party. The insurer must pay and then recover. This confirms that failing to check (even where the driver has no licence) does not defeat the insurer's defence in the sense of avoiding payment to the claimant.
supporting.quote: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a special endorsement is required (e.g., for carrying hazardous goods), the owner has a duty under Rule 132(5) of the CMVR to ensure the driver holds the requisite endorsement. Absence of such endorsement is a breach entitling the insurer to pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The vehicle was a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The driver had a valid HGV/HTV licence but no special endorsement under Rule 9 CMVR. The court held the owner failed in his duty and granted pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the one case where the court specifically identified a positive duty on the owner (under Rule 132(5) CMVR) to verify a special endorsement. It shows that where the law specifically casts a duty on the owner to verify a particular licence condition, failure to do so is a breach — but still results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date. The insurer must pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, the accident was on 02-07-2008, and the licence was renewed on 04-07-2008. The court held the licence was not valid on the accident date but directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a lapsed licence (which the owner could have checked) results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer's defence succeeds in shifting ultimate burden to the owner.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: Swaran Singh's pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks under Section 149. It does NOT apply to own-damage claims or disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side (claimant) will not cite this — it helps the insurer. But the insurer's own counsel must be aware: if the claim is an own-damage claim (not a third-party claim), the pay-and-recover safety net disappears. The insurer can fully defend on licence grounds.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about own-damage claims and consumer forum disputes between insurer and insured. In third-party claims (which are the vast majority of motor accident cases), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover principle fully apply. The claimant will not be affected by this limitation.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any licence is a fundamental breach. The insurer is not directly liable but must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must still pay. This is the strongest case for the claimant on the 'pay first' point.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case confirms the insurer's ultimate right to recover from the owner. The insurer's defence is not 'defeated' — it succeeds in shifting the burden to the owner. The insurer pays only as a statutory conduit to protect the third party.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will rely heavily on this for the proposition that licence defects do not let the insurer off the hook to third parties. The insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case explicitly reaffirms that the breach must be 'on the part of the insured' — i.e., the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver. If the owner checked and the licence appeared genuine, there is no 'breach' at all, and the insurer cannot even recover. This cuts both ways.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid third-party liability merely because the driver of an LMV did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the owner's duty to verify does not extend to checking for specific endorsements or badges. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This actually helps the insurer's position on the scope of the owner's duty — it confirms the owner need not check for regulatory endorsements. The insurer's defence (that the owner should have checked for a badge) is weakened, but the insurer still gets pay-and-recover.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: An expired licence that is renewed later does not constitute a fundamental breach. The insurer is liable to third parties.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even an expired licence (which the owner could have spotted) does not defeat the claim. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case is distinguishable on timing — the licence was renewed shortly after the accident, and the court emphasised that the licensing authority cannot refuse renewal within 5 years. The insurer still gets recovery rights against the owner.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to reinforce the proposition that absence of a licence does not let the insurer off the hook. The insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position that pay-and-recover is the correct remedy. The insurer's defence succeeds in shifting ultimate liability to the owner. The main dispute in this case was about contributory negligence, not licence verification.

priority_arguments: Lead with the Lehru principle (as quoted in Chennamma/doc_027): the owner's duty is limited to checking whether the licence 'on the face of it looks genuine'. The owner is NOT expected to verify with the RTO or investigate whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority.

Argue that if the owner checked the licence and it appeared genuine, and the driver demonstrated competence, there is NO breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii) at all — the insurer cannot even recover from the owner, let alone avoid liability.

In the alternative, argue that even if there IS a breach (e.g., no licence, fake licence, expired licence), the insurer's remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. This is settled law from Swaran Singh through to the present corpus.

Distinguish between third-party claims (where pay-and-recover applies) and own-damage claims (where Laxmi Narain Dhut/doc_031 limits Swaran Singh). In third-party claims, the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim.

Where the licence defect is a missing endorsement or badge (not absence of a licence altogether), rely on S.Iyyapan/doc_032 to argue that the owner cannot be expected to verify regulatory endorsements — the licence on its face was sufficient.

Where the licence had expired but was later renewed, rely on Srinivasamurthy/doc_034 and Parvathi Hebbar/doc_003 to argue that while there is a breach (licence not valid on accident date), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: The claimant will argue that the owner failed in his duty to verify the licence, and this constitutes a 'breach' that at least entitles the insurer to recover from the owner. If the owner is impecunious or untraceable, the insurer may be left bearing the loss despite having a recovery order.

In own-damage claims (not third-party), Laxmi Narain Dhut/doc_031 holds that Swaran Singh does not apply — the insurer can fully defend on licence grounds. Ensure the claim is properly characterised as a third-party claim.

If the owner did not check the licence AT ALL (e.g., hired a driver without asking for a licence), the court may find this is a 'willful' breach, strengthening the insurer's recovery rights but also potentially exposing the insurer to arguments that the owner was negligent.

The Sunil Shreesail Killiket/doc_024 case shows that even a 'fundamental breach' (no licence at all) results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer should not overstate the strength of its defence — it will have to pay first in third-party claims.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party motor accident claims before the MACT, the insurer should: (1) plead the licence defect specifically; (2) lead evidence to prove the defect (RTO verification report, MV Inspector testimony); (3) seek a pay-and-recover order against the owner/driver; (4) NOT argue for complete exoneration from third-party liability, as the corpus uniformly rejects this. In own-damage claims (consumer forum or civil suit), the insurer can take the full defence under Laxmi Narain Dhut.

caveats: The following judgments from the flagged list are NOT adverse on the licence-verification question and are excluded for the reasons stated: (a) doc_009 (Kamal) — concerns contributory negligence of the injured rider who himself drove without a licence; not about the owner's duty to check a driver's licence. (b) doc_016 (State of HP) — criminal case holding that absence of a licence does not itself constitute criminal negligence in driving; not about the owner's verification duty. (c) doc_017 (Sanjay) — criminal case about rash driving and identification of the driver; not about licence verification. (d) doc_014 (Shivlal), doc_028 (Sukumarbai), doc_029 (Minor Mahesh) — gratuitous passenger cases; not about licence verification. (e) doc_038 (Crown Consultants) — consumer dispute about delayed claim filing; unrelated. (f) doc_051 (Yashpal Chaudhrani) — criminal quashing for economic fraud; unrelated. (g) doc_054 (Chinnasamy) — specific performance suit; unrelated.

This analysis is limited to the 56-judgment corpus provided. Key Supreme Court precedents like Swaran Singh, Lehru, Skandia, and Sohan Lal Passi are cited within the corpus judgments but are not themselves part of the corpus. Their principles are applied through the corpus judgments.

The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely exonerated from third-party liability on licence grounds. Every licence-defect case in the corpus results in pay-and-recover. This may reflect a selection bias in the corpus rather than the full range of possible outcomes.

511 and also a judgement in the case of Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. J. Kotiratnama, 2000 (3) An.
W.R. 91.
On the other hand, learned counsel for the insurance company submits that the tractor was insured
but trolley was not insured. No premium was paid for the trolley as per Section 61 of the Motor

We have heard both the parties at length and gone through the material available on record.

payload.court: High Court of Jammu and Kashmir at Jammu
payload.holding: The court held that a legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency', reducing the total compensation accordingly.
payload.ratio: Only legal representatives who were dependent upon the victim at the time of death are entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'; non-dependent legal representatives can only claim under loss to estate and statutory liability under Section 140.

National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors. on 3
February, 2014

           HIGH COURT OF JAMMU AND KASHMIR
                       AT JAMMU
CIMA No. D-627/2010
CMA No. 933/2010
                                Date of decision:03.02.2014
  National Insurance Co. Ltd.    Vs. Harpreet Singh and others.
Coram:
        Hon'ble Mr. Justice Janak Raj Kotwal-Judge
Appearing counsel:
For appellant (s):      Mr. C. S. Gupta, Advocate
For respondent(s):      Mr. Surinder Singh, Advocate
i.     Whether approved for
       reporting in Press/Media  : Yes
ii.    Whether to be reported in
       Digest/Journal            : Yes
1. This is an appeal in a Motor Accident Claim case.
2. Heard. I have perused the record.
3. On 29.09.2007, S. Amarjeet Singh (hereinafter the deceased) was travelling from Kishtwar to
Jammu by a car bearing registration No. JK0 2D-9212. Respondent No. 3, Inderjit Singh Bali, who
was owner of the car, was on the wheel. The car met with an accident near a place called Thathri and
plunged into a trench. Deceased suffered grievous injuries. He died.
4. Respondent Nos. 1 & 2, (hereinafter the claimants) who are the sons of the deceased, filed a claim
for compensation under section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1998 (hereinafter the Act) before the
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Jammu (hereinafter the Tribunal) against the owner and insurer
(herein appellant) of the offending car.
5. Learned Tribunal vide its judgment and award dated 30.04.2010 found that the accident had
occurred due to rash and negligent driving by respondent No. 3 and awarded compensation of Rs.

ibunal, Jammu (hereinafter the Tribunal) against the owner and insurer
(herein appellant) of the offending car.
5. Learned Tribunal vide its judgment and award dated 30.04.2010 found that the accident had
occurred due to rash and negligent driving by respondent No. 3 and awarded compensation of Rs.

17,53,800/ to claimants. The Tribunal foisted liability of paying the compensation on the appellant.
6. In assessing the compensation, learned Tribunal on appreciation of evidence found that the
deceased was a Government servant serving as Manager QC in the Food Corporation of India. His
monthly salary was Rs. 24,149/. He was aged 54 years as at the time of his death. Learned Tribunal
deducted 1/3rd of the salary towards personal expenses of the deceased and took the remaining Rs.
16,100/ as his monthly contribution towards the claimants. Annual contribution of the deceased
towards the claimants thus came out as Rs. 1, 93,200/, which became the 'multiplicand' for
calculating compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'. On the basis of the age of the
deceased, applicable multiplier being 11, learned Tribunal scaled it down to 9. Compensation under
this head thus amounting to Rs. 17, 38, 800/ (1, 93,200x9). In addition, learned Tribunal awarded
Rs. 15,000/ as compensation for funeral expenses. Total compensation thus awarded was Rs. 17,
53,800/.
7. Appellant-Insurance Company has impugned the judgment and award of the learned Tribunal to
the extent of the quantum of compensation awarded to the claimants. Award has been assailed on
the ground that only respondent No. 2, who is a MBA student, should have been taken as dependent
of the deceased, whereas respondent No. 1 could not have been because he is gainfully employed as
per the evidence available before the Tribunal. It is also contended that as per the evidence, the
basic salary of the deceased was Rs. 10,600/ and the total amount which he was drawing after
deduction was Rs. 19,481/. It is also contended that both the claimants were major but this aspect
was ignored by the learned Tribunal.
8. Mr. C. S.

d Tribunal as
claimants' witness. In cross-examination he has admitted that his brother Harpreet Singh is
employed as a clerk in Doordarshan. This aspect is not disputed by the claimants. Appellant in its
objections before the learned Tribunal had clearly contended that the claimants were major and

earning hands. No evidence, however, has been led by the claimants to prove that even claimant
Harpreet Singh was an unemployed person and dependent upon the deceased up to the time of his
death. Since claimant, Harpreet Singh is gainfully employed in a Central Government service and
there is nothing in the claimants' evidence that he was dependent upon the deceased as at the time
of latter's death, appellant's contention that claimant Harpreet Singh cannot be taken as a person
dependent upon the deceased is to be accepted.
11. Viewed thus, correctness of compensation awarded under the head 'loss of dependency' by the
learned Tribunal calls for reconsideration. It needs to be determined, whether claimant, Harpreet
Singh, is entitled to the compensation under this head?
12. Before taking up the above aspect, I will however, first take up the appellant's challenge to the
correctness of the income of the deceased as taken by the learned Tribunal. In this regard, evidence
available with and relied upon by the learned Tribunal is the salary certificate Ex.PW KA issued by
Manager (Accounts), Food Corporation of India, District Office, Jammu. In this certificate, basic pay
of the deceased is shown as Rs. 10,600/ and total salary, inclusive of allowances as Rs. 24,149/.
Deduction towards CPF is shown as Rs. 4352/, Rs. 306/ is shown as deduction towards licensing fee
and Rs. 10/ towards BF. Learned Tribunal, therefore, cannot be said to have erred in taking total
salary of the deceased as Rs. 24,149/ because nothing except income tax paid on the total salary is
deductible, while ascertaining the contribution of the deceased towards his dependents.
13.

o
costs...."
23. The legal position, thus, can be summarized that a legal representative of a victim of a motor
accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is
not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'. He would be entitled to

compensation for loss to estate as well as the statutory compensation under section 140 of the Act.
24. Having stated the legal position as above, it can be said that learned Tribunal has erred in taking
respondent (claimant) Harpreet Singh too as a claimant entitled to get compensation under the
head 'loss of dependency' and in that taking strength of the family of the deceased as three and
deducting 1/3rd of the salary towards personal expenses of the deceased. Claimant-Harpreet Singh,
though a legal representative of the deceased and thereby entitled to lay the claim for compensation,
is not entitled to get compensation under the head 'loss of dependency' for the reason that he is
gainfully employed in Central Government service and was not dependent upon the deceased .
25. Strength of the family of the deceased for the purpose of 'loss of dependency' in this case should
have been and is being taken as two only and in applying the multiplier method, deduction towards
personal expenses of the deceased would be half of the salary. Since the deceased at the time of the
death was 50 plus, no addition to the income of the deceased is to be made. However, given that
total annual salary of the deceased was Rs. 2, 89,788/ (29149 x 12) and his savings, earning
deduction from taxable income was Rs. 52,224/ only so at least Rs. 15,000/ can be and should have
been deducted towards income tax. Effective income of the deceased should have been and is being
taken as Rs. 2, 74,788/- (2,89,788-15,000). Personal expenses of the deceased and his contribution
towards claimant-Harbaksh Singh for calculating compensation therefore, would be Rs. 1,37,394/
say Rs. 1,37,400/ each (half of Rs. 2,74,788/) each. This would be the 'multiplicand' in this case.
26. Deceased at the time of death was in the age group of 50 to 55. Applicable multiplier as per Sarla
Verma's case (supra) is 11.

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the licence appears genuine and the driver is competent, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner hired a driver who produced a licence with an LMV + transport vehicle endorsement. The court held the owner had done enough — he was not required to verify whether the endorsement covered the specific sub-class of heavy goods vehicle.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most directly applicable authority on the scope of the owner's verification duty. It quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 verbatim and applies it to hold that the owner's obligation is satisfied by a prima facie check of the licence document.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. ... Thus where the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently there would be no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory under Section 149. Even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), the insurer must pay the third party and can recover from the insured. The breach must be on the part of the insured — the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a valid licence to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The court still held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights, reaffirming that the breach must be 'willful' on the owner's part.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where there IS a licence defect, the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim — it only entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The owner's failure to check does not let the insurer off the hook to third parties.
supporting.quote: As held in Skandia and Sohan Lal Passi cases the breach must be on the part of the insured. ... If it ultimately turns out that the licence was fake, the insurance company would continue to remain liable unless they prove that the owner/insured was aware or had noticed that the licence was fake and still permitted that person to drive.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds a valid LMV licence but lacks a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle, the insurer cannot avoid third-party liability. The owner is not expected to know the fine distinctions between licence classes.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had an LMV licence but no badge/endorsement for a tourist maxi cab (commercial vehicle). The Supreme Court held the insurer liable, rejecting the argument that the owner should have checked for the endorsement.
supporting.why_it_matters: Limits the owner's verification duty: the owner need not check for specific endorsements or badges that are matters of regulatory detail. A licence that on its face authorises the relevant class of vehicle is sufficient.
supporting.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: An expired licence that is subsequently renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer remains liable and must pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed later. The court held the insurer liable to third parties, finding no fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even where the licence had lapsed (a clear defect an owner could have spotted by checking the expiry date), the insurer's defence does not succeed against third parties. The owner's failure to notice an expired licence does not defeat the claim.
supporting.quote: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no badge for tourist maxi cab. The court applied pay-and-recover, holding the insurer liable to the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the owner failed to ensure the driver had the correct endorsement/badge, the insurer's defence does not defeat the third-party claim — it only shifts the ultimate burden to the owner via recovery.
supporting.quote: The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any licence at all is a fundamental and statutory breach. However, even in such cases, the insurer must pay the third party first and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal found a fundamental breach but still applied pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — does not allow the insurer to escape liability to the third party. The insurer must pay and then recover. This confirms that failing to check (even where the driver has no licence) does not defeat the insurer's defence in the sense of avoiding payment to the claimant.
supporting.quote: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a special endorsement is required (e.g., for carrying hazardous goods), the owner has a duty under Rule 132(5) of the CMVR to ensure the driver holds the requisite endorsement. Absence of such endorsement is a breach entitling the insurer to pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The vehicle was a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The driver had a valid HGV/HTV licence but no special endorsement under Rule 9 CMVR. The court held the owner failed in his duty and granted pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the one case where the court specifically identified a positive duty on the owner (under Rule 132(5) CMVR) to verify a special endorsement. It shows that where the law specifically casts a duty on the owner to verify a particular licence condition, failure to do so is a breach — but still results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date. The insurer must pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, the accident was on 02-07-2008, and the licence was renewed on 04-07-2008. The court held the licence was not valid on the accident date but directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a lapsed licence (which the owner could have checked) results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer's defence succeeds in shifting ultimate burden to the owner.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: Swaran Singh's pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks under Section 149. It does NOT apply to own-damage claims or disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side (claimant) will not cite this — it helps the insurer. But the insurer's own counsel must be aware: if the claim is an own-damage claim (not a third-party claim), the pay-and-recover safety net disappears. The insurer can fully defend on licence grounds.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about own-damage claims and consumer forum disputes between insurer and insured. In third-party claims (which are the vast majority of motor accident cases), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover principle fully apply. The claimant will not be affected by this limitation.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any licence is a fundamental breach. The insurer is not directly liable but must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must still pay. This is the strongest case for the claimant on the 'pay first' point.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case confirms the insurer's ultimate right to recover from the owner. The insurer's defence is not 'defeated' — it succeeds in shifting the burden to the owner. The insurer pays only as a statutory conduit to protect the third party.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will rely heavily on this for the proposition that licence defects do not let the insurer off the hook to third parties. The insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case explicitly reaffirms that the breach must be 'on the part of the insured' — i.e., the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver. If the owner checked and the licence appeared genuine, there is no 'breach' at all, and the insurer cannot even recover. This cuts both ways.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid third-party liability merely because the driver of an LMV did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the owner's duty to verify does not extend to checking for specific endorsements or badges. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This actually helps the insurer's position on the scope of the owner's duty — it confirms the owner need not check for regulatory endorsements. The insurer's defence (that the owner should have checked for a badge) is weakened, but the insurer still gets pay-and-recover.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: An expired licence that is renewed later does not constitute a fundamental breach. The insurer is liable to third parties.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even an expired licence (which the owner could have spotted) does not defeat the claim. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case is distinguishable on timing — the licence was renewed shortly after the accident, and the court emphasised that the licensing authority cannot refuse renewal within 5 years. The insurer still gets recovery rights against the owner.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to reinforce the proposition that absence of a licence does not let the insurer off the hook. The insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position that pay-and-recover is the correct remedy. The insurer's defence succeeds in shifting ultimate liability to the owner. The main dispute in this case was about contributory negligence, not licence verification.

priority_arguments: Lead with the Lehru principle (as quoted in Chennamma/doc_027): the owner's duty is limited to checking whether the licence 'on the face of it looks genuine'. The owner is NOT expected to verify with the RTO or investigate whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority.

Argue that if the owner checked the licence and it appeared genuine, and the driver demonstrated competence, there is NO breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii) at all — the insurer cannot even recover from the owner, let alone avoid liability.

In the alternative, argue that even if there IS a breach (e.g., no licence, fake licence, expired licence), the insurer's remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. This is settled law from Swaran Singh through to the present corpus.

Distinguish between third-party claims (where pay-and-recover applies) and own-damage claims (where Laxmi Narain Dhut/doc_031 limits Swaran Singh). In third-party claims, the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim.

Where the licence defect is a missing endorsement or badge (not absence of a licence altogether), rely on S.Iyyapan/doc_032 to argue that the owner cannot be expected to verify regulatory endorsements — the licence on its face was sufficient.

Where the licence had expired but was later renewed, rely on Srinivasamurthy/doc_034 and Parvathi Hebbar/doc_003 to argue that while there is a breach (licence not valid on accident date), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: The claimant will argue that the owner failed in his duty to verify the licence, and this constitutes a 'breach' that at least entitles the insurer to recover from the owner. If the owner is impecunious or untraceable, the insurer may be left bearing the loss despite having a recovery order.

In own-damage claims (not third-party), Laxmi Narain Dhut/doc_031 holds that Swaran Singh does not apply — the insurer can fully defend on licence grounds. Ensure the claim is properly characterised as a third-party claim.

If the owner did not check the licence AT ALL (e.g., hired a driver without asking for a licence), the court may find this is a 'willful' breach, strengthening the insurer's recovery rights but also potentially exposing the insurer to arguments that the owner was negligent.

result.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the licence appears genuine and the driver is competent, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner hired a driver who produced a licence with an LMV + transport vehicle endorsement. The court held the owner had done enough — he was not required to verify whether the endorsement covered the specific sub-class of heavy goods vehicle.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most directly applicable authority on the scope of the owner's verification duty. It quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 verbatim and applies it to hold that the owner's obligation is satisfied by a prima facie check of the licence document.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory under Section 149. Even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), the insurer must pay the third party and can recover from the insured. The breach must be on the part of the insured — the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a valid licence to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The court still held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights, reaffirming that the breach must be 'willful' on the owner's part.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where there IS a licence defect, the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim — it only entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The owner's failure to check does not let the insurer off the hook to third parties.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds a valid LMV licence but lacks a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle, the insurer cannot avoid third-party liability. The owner is not expected to know the fine distinctions between licence classes.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had an LMV licence but no badge/endorsement for a tourist maxi cab (commercial vehicle). The Supreme Court held the insurer liable, rejecting the argument that the owner should have checked for the endorsement.
supporting.why_it_matters: Limits the owner's verification duty: the owner need not check for specific endorsements or badges that are matters of regulatory detail. A licence that on its face authorises the relevant class of vehicle is sufficient.
supporting.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: An expired licence that is subsequently renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer remains liable and must pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed later. The court held the insurer liable to third parties, finding no fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even where the licence had lapsed (a clear defect an owner could have spotted by checking the expiry date), the insurer's defence does not succeed against third parties. The owner's failure to notice an expired licence does not defeat the claim.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no badge for tourist maxi cab. The court applied pay-and-recover, holding the insurer liable to the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the owner failed to ensure the driver had the correct endorsement/badge, the insurer's defence does not defeat the third-party claim — it only shifts the ultimate burden to the owner via recovery.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any licence at all is a fundamental and statutory breach. However, even in such cases, the insurer must pay the third party first and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal found a fundamental breach but still applied pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — does not allow the insurer to escape liability to the third party. The insurer must pay and then recover. This confirms that failing to check (even where the driver has no licence) does not defeat the insurer's defence in the sense of avoiding payment to the claimant.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a special endorsement is required (e.g., for carrying hazardous goods), the owner has a duty under Rule 132(5) of the CMVR to ensure the driver holds the requisite endorsement. Absence of such endorsement is a breach entitling the insurer to pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The vehicle was a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The driver had a valid HGV/HTV licence but no special endorsement under Rule 9 CMVR. The court held the owner failed in his duty and granted pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the one case where the court specifically identified a positive duty on the owner (under Rule 132(5) CMVR) to verify a special endorsement. It shows that where the law specifically casts a duty on the owner to verify a particular licence condition, failure to do so is a breach — but still results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date. The insurer must pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, the accident was on 02-07-2008, and the licence was renewed on 04-07-2008. The court held the licence was not valid on the accident date but directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a lapsed licence (which the owner could have checked) results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The insurer's defence succeeds in shifting ultimate burden to the owner.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: Swaran Singh's pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks under Section 149. It does NOT apply to own-damage claims or disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side (claimant) will not cite this — it helps the insurer. But the insurer's own counsel must be aware: if the claim is an own-damage claim (not a third-party claim), the pay-and-recover safety net disappears. The insurer can fully defend on licence grounds.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about own-damage claims and consumer forum disputes between insurer and insured. In third-party claims (which are the vast majority of motor accident cases), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover principle fully apply. The claimant will not be affected by this limitation.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any licence is a fundamental breach. The insurer is not directly liable but must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must still pay. This is the strongest case for the claimant on the 'pay first' point.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case confirms the insurer's ultimate right to recover from the owner. The insurer's defence is not 'defeated' — it succeeds in shifting the burden to the owner. The insurer pays only as a statutory conduit to protect the third party.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will rely heavily on this for the proposition that licence defects do not let the insurer off the hook to third parties. The insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case explicitly reaffirms that the breach must be 'on the part of the insured' — i.e., the owner must have knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver. If the owner checked and the licence appeared genuine, there is no 'breach' at all, and the insurer cannot even recover. This cuts both ways.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid third-party liability merely because the driver of an LMV did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the owner's duty to verify does not extend to checking for specific endorsements or badges. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This actually helps the insurer's position on the scope of the owner's duty — it confirms the owner need not check for regulatory endorsements. The insurer's defence (that the owner should have checked for a badge) is weakened, but the insurer still gets pay-and-recover.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: An expired licence that is renewed later does not constitute a fundamental breach. The insurer is liable to third parties.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even an expired licence (which the owner could have spotted) does not defeat the claim. The insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case is distinguishable on timing — the licence was renewed shortly after the accident, and the court emphasised that the licensing authority cannot refuse renewal within 5 years. The insurer still gets recovery rights against the owner.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to reinforce the proposition that absence of a licence does not let the insurer off the hook. The insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position that pay-and-recover is the correct remedy. The insurer's defence succeeds in shifting ultimate liability to the owner. The main dispute in this case was about contributory negligence, not licence verification.
